fixes.explanation: Two hundred fifty, baker! The text calls them men of Israel "renowned as leaders of the congregation and representatives in the assembly." (Numbers 16:2) These aren't strangers wandering in off the road. These are the folks with name tags that people actually recognize. Korah brings 250 big names to one complaint, and Moses has to look at every single one of them.

Before Moses says one word back, he falls facedown. Most of us would be busy loading up a comeback, friend. The text doesn't tell us why he does it, and I'm not going to guess for it. It just says, "When Moses heard this, he fell facedown." (Numbers 16:4) His words to Korah and all his followers come after.

That's the charge. Dathan and Abiram ask, "Must you also appoint yourself as ruler over us?" (Numbers 16:13) Watch that little word "also." They've just said Moses brought them up to kill them in the wilderness, and now they pile this on top. That's a whole lot of accusation for one breath, friend. It's like someone who hands you a full list of complaints and then says, "Oh, and another thing."

A donkey is the answer. Moses tells the LORD, "I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them." (Numbers 16:15) The text says Moses is very angry when he says it, right after asking the LORD not to regard their offering. He's saying he hasn't taken even one from them. The text doesn't say why he names a donkey, so I'll just leave it right there.

A flood would be quite a headline, friend, but Moses never mentions water. The sign he names is that "the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and all that belongs to them." (Numbers 16:30) The ground itself is what moves, not a river. I think this is a heavy part of the passage, and it's good to read it slowly.

No storm in this one, baker. Nothing falls from the sky and no wind blows in Moses' words. He says it's something "unprecedented," and then he spells it out: the earth opens its mouth, and they go down alive into Sheol. (Numbers 16:30) It's a heavy part of the passage, so I'll say it plainly and not dress it up.

True, baker. The next day, the whole congregation of Israel grumbles against Moses and Aaron, saying, "You have killed the LORD's people!" (Numbers 16:41) Think about that. After everything they just watched, the grumbling starts right back up. I think this one is heavy, and it shows how quickly the complaining comes back.
